current_flow: statement-export-api serves POST api/mis/statement/export behind AuthGuard plus RequireAction('report') under the global CSRF guard, with typed Swagger and a CORS exposedHeaders entry so the filename is readable. It calls MisStatementService.run ONCE and branches before any header: resolved streams a workbook named from lowercase slugs of the resolved scope, unresolvable returns ordinary JSON with no file headers. The writer receives that one payload and never re-queries or re-derives; it writes worksheet 'Financial MIS' with merged identity and per-block header groups, data in preorder with Excel outline levels, and a merged Grand Total row. Amounts are numbers rounded to the rupee so the sheet matches the screen, percentages are numbers, verbatim labels or NA, one header group per present block, and every text cell from the uploaded workbook is neutralised against formula injection.
new_abstractions: a canonical slug filename derived from resolved scope, not raw input
a pinned worksheet layout with Excel outline levels so the hierarchy survives
formula-injection neutralisation on text originating in a client workbook

gaps: The plan's workflow diagram still said SessionGuard while the statement route uses AuthGuard plus RequireAction('report') - I had corrected this in the criteria but the diagram kept the wrong guard, a direct contradiction inside one document.

Surface Impact promised a mis-statement.service.ts refactor that is both outside the write scope and unnecessary: the service already returns the assembled response, so the export route simply calls it once.

'Convert FixedScaleMoney directly, never via the display-rounded value' contradicted the confirmed rule that rounding happens after aggregation for display AND export, and left the cell-equality test with no declared presentation to assert.

The browser cannot read Content-Disposition from the cross-origin credentialed fetch the next task will use: CORS does not expose it by default, and backend/src/main.ts was outside the write scope, so the filename would have been unreadable.
Swagger proof was incomplete: decision 0019 requires the strict selector schema and typed 400/401/403 responses, and no required leaf asserted Swagger or the CSRF header.

'Streams an xlsx' is not enough to prevent a corrupt download: the route must branch on run()'s outcome BEFORE setting any header, so an unresolvable request returns ordinary JSON with neither file headers nor an xlsx body.
The plan promised contract and DTO changes but named no new shape - the request schema and the JSON unresolvable DTO already exist, and the workbook is bytes rather than a typed response.

Spreadsheet formula injection was unaddressed: S. No., component names and GL text all originate in an uploaded client workbook, and a value beginning =, +, - or @ reopens as a formula in the artifact people are sent.

The gated test registration must appear exactly once in backend/package.json and once in tools/quality-gate.test.mjs, which verifies those lists exactly; Manual Verification also still spoke of four required leaves.
'Sanitized canonical filename naming scope and range' had no testable grammar, and 'range' was ambiguous because a July request carries both a July block and a YTD block.
'Cell by cell' was not falsifiable without a stable worksheet name, row positions, merge ranges or total-row shape.
The contract said only that non-numeric percentages are verbatim - it never said whether a numeric ratio is an Excel number or text, nor how null is represented.

The first criterion now requires Swagger to document the xlsx content type, the Content-Disposition header, the JSON unresolvable outcome, the CSRF header and decision 0019's typed 400/401/403 responses.

The second criterion requires the route to call run() ONCE and branch on its outcome BEFORE setting any header, with the unresolvable path returning ordinary 200 application/json with no file headers and no xlsx body - and a required leaf asserts exactly that.
Surface Impact now states that contract/src/api.ts is NOT touched: the request schema and JSON unresolvable DTO already exist and the workbook is bytes.

A FIFTH acceptance criterion and a fourth required leaf require every text cell originating in an uploaded workbook to be neutralised, and reviewer_focus names formula injection as the security lens's main object here.
backend/package.json and tools/quality-gate.test.mjs are in the write scope with reviewer_focus requiring exactly one registration in each, and Manual Verification now matches the leaf count.

The filename grammar is pinned: financial-mis-<department>-<function>-<plant>-<active-from>-to-<active-to>.xlsx, from lowercase ASCII slugs of the RESOLVED scope rather than raw input, where the active block is 'selected' or the only block.

The layout is pinned: worksheet 'Financial MIS', row 1 merged identity and per-block header groups, row 2 column labels, data from row 3 in preorder with root outline level 1, and a final row merging the three identity cells as Grand Total - with the test REOPENING the generated bytes rather than inspecting the writer.

The fourth criterion now states all three percentage paths: a numeric ratio is a number with a percentage format, a label is literal text verbatim, and null is the literal NA, each asserted after reopening the workbook.

rounds.question: The grill found a contradiction in my export plan about the numbers in the spreadsheet. The spec says amounts are 'rounded to the rupee' for display, and the screen shows ₹1,00,50,136. But the underlying payload carries exact paise (10050136.29). Someone reconciling the sheet against SAP would want the paise; someone checking it against the screen would want them to match exactly. What should the exported cells contain?
options: Rounded to the rupee, matching the screen (Recommended)
Rounded values, with a paise-exact column alongside

summary: One cold read returned twelve findings and blocked the handover. It caught a contradiction I had half-fixed: the criteria named the right guards but the workflow diagram still said SessionGuard, which is the frontend's. It caught a promised refactor of a file that neither needs nor permits one, a contract change with no named shape, and - importantly - that the browser cannot read Content-Disposition at all without a CORS exposedHeaders entry in main.ts, which was outside the scope. It also found the export had no formula-injection protection, though every text cell originates in a client-supplied workbook and the export is precisely the artifact people forward. Three specifications were pinned so 'cell by cell' became falsifiable: the filename grammar from resolved-scope slugs, the worksheet layout down to merge ranges and outline levels with the test REOPENING the generated bytes, and all three percentage paths. The one genuine product question went to the human: exported amounts are numbers ROUNDED TO THE RUPEE so the sheet matches the screen line for line, with the rounding cost named rather than hidden. Verdict pass.
